summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, and Yihao Yang

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study introduces a framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics, overcoming the limitations of 2D systems which suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. The authors theoretically and experimentally demonstrate a 3D photonic crystal with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, this 3D system features triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors. This vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states on all sample surfaces. The research verifies the vectorial Berry curvature using pump-probe measurements and demonstrates that the propagation direction of these surface states is intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule relative to the valley Chern vectors. These findings open new avenues for 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging applications across various frequency ranges.

Research Context
Prior valley photonics was restricted to two dimensions. 2D systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and planar confinement. Full 3D confinement requires a complete photonic bandgap. Existing 3D topological insulators lack surface states on all surfaces.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can 3D valley photonics be realized with a complete bandgap? Do 3D systems exhibit vectorial valley-contrasting physics? Can chiral surface states exist on all surfaces of a 3D sample? Is the propagation governed by the right-hand-thumb rule?

Methodological Details
The study uses a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm. The crystal structure is a photonic diamond with PEC spheres and rods. Each fcc cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm. Inversion symmetry is broken by setting D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm. The experiment operates at a frequency of 13.8 GHz for selective excitation. Surface states are observed at 14.6 GHz. The (001) surface is covered by a metallic plate to tune boundary conditions. Key boundary parameters are h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm.

Procedures And Architectures
The effective Hamiltonian is derived using the k · p method. Valley states are selectively excited using a vectorial chiral source array. The source array consists of four sources with specific relative positions. Phase delays are set to (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+. Valley Chern vectors are calculated by integrating the Berry curvature. Surface states are verified by measuring surface transmission and field distribution. Fourier transforms are applied to map surface dispersion and isofrequency contours. The right-hand-thumb rule is verified by observing propagation loops on different surfaces.

Key Results
Breaking inversion symmetry opens a complete photonic bandgap. The system exhibits six valleys grouped into triple pairs. Berry curvature components verify vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Valley Chern vectors are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). Selective excitation shows outcoupling directions of −32.9° and +32.9°. Surface transmission remains high within the complete photonic bandgap. Surface states exhibit nearly-linear dispersion in the bandgap. Surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction. Surface states circulate on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. Transmission remains high through sharp corners due to valley conservation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature allows for vectorial bulk valley vortices. Surface states are canalized due to flat isofrequency contours. The right-hand-thumb rule relates VCVs to circulating propagation. This enables unprecedented 3D guiding and trapping of light. The concept extends to terahertz and optical ranges.

Contradictions And Limitations
Demonstration is currently at lower frequencies (microwave). Boundary conditions require specific metallic plate tuning. Fabrication relies on perfect electric conductor (PEC) approximations.

Claims
3D topological valley photonics supports canalized chiral surface states on all surfaces governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. Surface states propagate on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces. Propagation direction obeys the right-hand-thumb rule. Valley conservation allows smooth passage through corners. Existing 3D topological insulators only support states on certain surfaces. Enables 3D waveguiding and directional radiation.
Vectorial valley-contrasting physics allows selective excitation of specific valley states. Outcoupling directions match theoretical predictions. Phase winding controls the outcoupling direction. 2D radiation patterns diverge in the vertical direction. Provides opportunities for directional antenna design.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Robustness is demonstrated by high transmission through sharp corners. Canalization is confirmed by flat isofrequency contours.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the 3D VPC structure and band structure. Figure 2 shows selective excitation and outcoupling directions. Figure 3 demonstrates canalized chiral valley surface states. Figure 4 illustrates the right-hand-thumb rule and corner propagation.

Three Takeaways
1. Development of 3D topological valley photonics with complete bandgap. 2. Observation of canalized chiral surface states on all surfaces. 3. Verification of the right-hand-thumb rule for valley propagation.
